title: Coming back after a lapse
hook: a Sikh who breaks rehat can return through penance and a fresh start

segments.voice: Yesterday, rehat as love: two students, one piece, and the difference only they could hear. Your line was kept in love. Which chore did you do for someone underneath it? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-five.

A piece of paper, folded and kept. On it, a few lines that say, in effect: you are not our Guru, and we are not your Sikhs. Sikh tradition tells of a band of men from the Majha region who wrote a letter like that during the long siege of Anandpur, signed it, handed it to Guru Gobind Singh, and went home. The word for that letter is bedava, a disclaimer. Tradition says the Guru kept it. They had walked away, in writing. Earlier in this block we met the penance the five set when the code is broken, and how it often takes the form of service. Today isn't about the penance. It's about what happens to that piece of paper.
screen: `A LETTER: YOU ARE NOT OUR GURU.` → `SIGNED, HANDED OVER, GONE HOME.` → `WHAT HAPPENS TO THE PAPER?`

segments.voice: Here's how the story is told. At home, the men are met with shame instead of welcome. A woman named Mai Bhago will not let it rest. Tradition says she rode out with them, back toward the Guru, and they caught up with his pursuers near a pool called Khidrana. They fought there, and they fell. When the Guru came over the field, he found one of them, Mahan Singh, still breathing, and lifted his head into his lap. The dying man asked for one thing: tear up the letter. And the Guru took out the bedava and tore it. Sikhs remember those men as the Mukte, the liberated, and the place is called Muktsar. They are remembered in the Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh gatherings. Now set the code beside the story. The Rehat Maryada says, in paraphrase, that a Sikh who breaks the rehat should come before the five, admit it plainly, accept the penance they set, and, where amrit has been broken, take it again. Then the person begins fresh. The way the code lays it out, the procedure is a way back in. And the story says the same thing in another key. The men didn't come back by arguing they'd been right. They came back, and they gave everything. The paper that said we are not your Sikhs wasn't filed away as evidence. The Guru tore it. So this week ends here. We met the kirpan and the law, the kara and the comb, food, a clear mind, faithfulness at home, and rehat as love. Today, the door that stays open when any of them is broken.
screen: `MAI BHAGO RIDES THEM BACK.` · `THE GURU TEARS THE LETTER.` · `THE CODE: ADMIT, ACCEPT, BEGIN AGAIN.` · then, large: `THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome someone back. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who drifted away from you, or from a family, a team, a friendship, or a faith community you belong to. Maybe they left loudly. Maybe they just stopped coming. Hold them in your mind without rehearsing the argument. Then picture one small, real way to make coming back easier for them: a message, a seat saved, a plain hello. You don't have to send it now. Just let the welcome be ready. The bell holds the time.

Coming back after a lapse. In the Sikh code, one who breaks rehat comes before the five, accepts a penance, and starts fresh. In the story of Muktsar, the Guru tears up the letter that said goodbye. Today's word.
screen: `COMING BACK AFTER A LAPSE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: you can return. Today, go back to one good habit you've let slip, without making a speech about it. Just pick it up again. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: A Sikh who has broken the rehat appears before five amritdhari Sikhs, admits the lapse, and accepts a penance (tankhah); where amrit has been broken, it is taken again. The story of the Mukte of Muktsar is told as a picture of return.

notes: The Muktsar story is told as tradition. Details to confirm: the men came from the Majha region; they signed the bedava during the siege of Anandpur; Mai Bhago led them back; the pool/place was Khidrana; the dying Sikh was Mahan Singh; the Guru tore the letter. The traditional count of forty (Chali Mukte) is deliberately not stated under the claims rule.
'They are remembered in the Ardas': the Ardas names 'the forty liberated' (chali muktian); please confirm, and that describing the Ardas as said at the close of Sikh gatherings is acceptable.
The code's procedure (appear before the five, confess, accept tankhah, retake amrit where broken) is paraphrased; please confirm.
Week-end day (1289–1295): the teach closes with a one-line look back at the week's subjects.
Days 1274–1275 covered penance and penance as service; this day takes the angle of welcome and the torn letter to avoid repeating them.

Editor pass (1292-1301): the absolute claim 'no line in the code says a door closes for good' replaced with a statement about how the code's procedure reads, since it could not be checked against the whole code.
